title: Adaptive fallback cost model & synthetic load calibration - lab log
body:
Context
---
Quick personal log. Trying to get an experimental, low-friction calibration approach for our 'fallback' behavior (when primary model or dedicated pool is unavailable) that balances tail latency SLOs and token/unit cost. Goal: a lightweight cost model + synthetic load generator so product & runtime teams can tune routing policies without full cluster tests.

Motivation and high-level idea
---
Current situation: fallback routes (cheaper model variant or remote region) kick in automatically based on availability and simple heuristics (latency threshold, error count). We lack a principled way to quantify the unit cost tradeoff vs increased tail-latency risk for specific tenant workloads.

Proposed: Build an "Adaptive Fallback Cost Model" (AFCM) that simulates request flows with configurable prefetch/caching, fallback policies, and per-route cost/latency distributions. Feed it lightweight real telemetry histograms to calibrate. Then run targeted synthetic load experiments to find operating points (e.g., target p99 <= X ms while minimizing expected tokens-cost).

Key primitives and signals to model
---
- arrival_profile: inter-arrival distribution (mixed Poisson + bursts). Represent as histogram or parametric (lambda, burst_prob, burst_mean).
- request_shape: {prompt_len, response_len_target, streaming_enabled, kv_hit_prob} encoded as summary stats (med, p90, p99).
- route_variants: an array of candidate routes. For each: latency_distribution (empirical histogram), cost_per_token, cold_start_ms (tail contributor), success_rate.
- prefetch_cache: prefix-KV cache hit probability and warmup effectiveness (reduces compute tokens by factor f_hit).
- fallback_policy: rule-set describing when to fall back. Examples: (A) simple latency threshold (if estimated remaining time > T -> fallback), (B) conservative: fallback if any upstream error or queue depth > Q, (C) quality-aware: fallback only for stateless prompts or when cached answer exists.
- circuit_state: transient metrics that determine whether fallback is allowed (e.g., tenant_burst_allowed=false for 30s after N failures).

Model outputs (things we want to measure)
---
- expected_cost_per_1000_requests (tokens*cost + infra surcharge)
- latency percentiles p50/p90/p99 at candidate SLOs
- fallback_frequency and fallback-induced-quality-drop (approx metric: fraction of requests served by cheaper variant)
- cold-start penalty contributions to p99
- cost variance (important for billing predictability)

Calibration approach
---
1) Ingest real telemetry exports (from Console): per-route latency histograms, token counts, per-request metadata (boolean flags: cached, streamed). Use aggregated daily snapshots (median, p90, p99, mean tokens).
2) Fit simple parametric families: log-normal for latencies, geometric/Pareto for burst inter-arrivals. Keep fitting light-weight (no heavy Bayesian).
3) Adjust per-route cost_per_token from pricing matrix + quantization profile.

Synthetic load generator (design notes)
---
- Generator modes: steady-state (constant lambda), burst (lambda spikes with configurable duration and multiplier), real-trace-replay (replay sampled request traces including KV-hit labels).
- Must support request attributes: prompt_len, streaming flag, route affinity hints (region preference).
- Implement as a small Go binary (reuse ingress-sim code) that emits either gRPC or HTTP requests to a local simulator endpoint. Simulator accepts 'fast-forward' mode (run a 1h simulated workload in 5s).

Simulator architecture (text diagram)
---
[request-gen] -> [ingress-queue model] -> [router] -> [route-exec model (per-variant latency sampler + cost counter)] -> [cache-layer model (prefix hits)] -> [metrics sink]

Router logic pseudocode (simplified)
---
if route.primary.available == false:
  choose route.fallback
else if estimated_remaining_time(route.primary) > latency_threshold and fallback_allowed:
  choose route.fallback
else:
  choose route.primary

`estimated_remaining_time` uses a queueing estimate: latency_mean + queue_depth * per_request_service_time_estimate.

Experiment matrix (initial)
---
- Dimensions:
  - arrival_profile: steady (100 rps), burst (100->1k rps, 30s), trace-sampled
  - fallback_policy: threshold T in {50ms, 100ms, 200ms}, conservative, quality-aware
  - prefetch_cache: hit_rate in {0.0, 0.2, 0.5}
  - route variants: primary=A40-quant, fallback=B6-quant-low, remote-high-latency
- Metrics to capture per run: p50/p90/p99 latency, average cost, fallback_rate, failure_rate, coldstart_count

Decision heuristics we can derive
---
- If cache_hit_rate > 0.4, favor raising fallback threshold (more primary usage yields lower marginal cost and better quality).
- If burstiness_coefficient > 2.0 (lots of spiky traffic), tune conservative fallback early to protect p99 but accept higher cost for short windows.
- Define "cost per avoided p99-ms" metric: delta_cost / delta_p99_ms. Use as knob to choose threshold.

Edge cases and caveats
---
- Quality regressions: cheaper fallback may produce hallucinations. SLO math only covers latency/cost; we need to layer in eval-set regressions as a penalty term. For now, surface fallback_rate to CS/product and map to manual thresholds.
- Nonstationary traffic: calibration becomes stale rapidly for app with daily/weekly patterns. Plan nightly recalibration with last-24h telemetry.
- Telemetry noise: tail samples are sparse; use smoothing or bootstrap to estimate p99 confidence intervals.

Rollout plan for a tenant (manual first)
---
1) Run simulation with tenant's telemetry to pick candidate threshold T and policy.
2) Run local synthetic replay against small percentage of live traffic in canary mode (e.g., 2% of traffic mirrored to simulator path with no user-visible effect) to validate.
3) Gradual ramp: 5% of traffic with live fallback enabled (and sticky fallback logging). Monitor p99 + downstream quality signals for 48h.
4) If stable, adopt policy in route config; schedule daily recalibration job.

Open implementation tasks (personal checklist)
---
- [ ] extract minimal telemetry export script (console -> json histograms)
- [ ] light-weight simulator endpoint (reuse ingress-sim, add 'fast-forward' semantics)
- [ ] dashboard prototype: overlay cost vs p99 curves for chosen tenant
- [ ] small canary orchestration: mirror to simulator, record divergences
- [ ] simple quality penalty integration: map fallback route to a base penalty score (manual) until eval integration exists

Notes from quick experiments (toy results)
---
- With synthetic steady 200 rps and fallback threshold 100ms, fallback_rate=12%, avg_cost down 8%, p99 up by 60ms.
- With cache_hit_rate=0.5, same policy -> fallback_rate drops to 4%, avg_cost neutral, p99 stable.
- Cold-start tail (rare) dominates p99 in burst tests; adding a soft-bounded warm pool (allow 1 warm idle instance per 100 tenants) reduced cold-start contribution by ~40% in sim.

Questions / things to validate with SRE/product
---
- How to map a fallback route to an official "quality score" that product teams accept? (manual mapping vs eval-integration)
- What is acceptable billing volatility to finance for enterprise tenants? (we can compute cost variance but need thresholds)
- Do we expose this policy as tenant-configurable in Console, or keep as platform-managed?

Appendix: quick param defaults for initial sim
---
- default_service_time_primary_mean = 40ms; stdev=1.5x
- default_service_time_fallback_mean = 65ms; stdev=1.6x
- cost_primary = $0.0009 per token-equivalent; cost_fallback = $0.00045
- KV_prefetch_hit_effect = 0.35 token reduction on average
- coldstart_latency = 200ms spike (probability 0.01 per request during bursts)

Next actions (next week)
---
- pull telemetry for 3 representative mid-market tenants and run baseline sim
- prototype dashboard plot: x-axis threshold T, y1=p99 latency, y2=avg cost (dual y)
- sync with SRE about cheap warm-pool feasibility

-- end of lab log (Maya)
